evidence_set: The authors write that the genetic approach strongly supports the hypothesis that cannabis use is causally related to the risk of schizophrenia, and call it additional evidence that cannabis use is likely to increase that risk; the abstract prints P = 0.007, the p-value of the per-unit estimate, beside the rescaled odds ratio of 1.37 for people who use against people who do not. They note that the variants did not reach genome-wide significance and that, with non-overlapping exposure and outcome data, weak-instrument bias would bias the estimate towards the null.
Abstract; Results › Causal effect of ever use of cannabis on risk of schizophrenia, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st, 4th and 5th paragraphs

The authors read their results as weak evidence for a causal link from cannabis use to schizophrenia and much stronger evidence for a causal link from schizophrenia to cannabis use (the 2019 correction re-worded several such uses of 'schizophrenia' as liability to schizophrenia or schizophrenia risk, without listing them), suggest that people at risk may experience prodromal symptoms or negative affect that lead them to start using cannabis to cope or self-medicate, contrast this with Vaucher et al. and align it with Gage et al. (2017), and suggest that the weak forward evidence may be due to the lower power of the cannabis instruments.
Discussion, 7th paragraph; Author Correction, Nat Neurosci 2019;22(7):1196, doi 10.1038/s41593-019-0402-7 (PubMed abstract)

evidence_set: Nausea and vomiting due to chemotherapy: 28 studies (37 reports; 1772 participants): 14 nabilone, 3 dronabinol, 1 nabiximols, 4 levonantradol, 6 THC; 8 placebo-controlled (3 with an active arm as well) and 20 against an active drug only; the most common active comparator was prochlorperazine (15 studies, counting 2 three-arm trials that also had placebo); risk of bias high in 23, unclear in 5. Complete response, cannabinoid (dronabinol or nabiximols) against placebo: OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42), 3 trials, 102 patients, I2 0%, GRADE low; the abstract gives 47% against 20%, a figure not derived in the article (study card reporting issue). No pooled comparison with active drugs is reported.

evidence_set: Figure 2: 254 of 685 people with cannabinoids and 215 of 685 with placebo had at least 30% less pain across the 8 trials (37.1% and 31.4%, the abstract's 37% and 31%; editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), I2 47.6%; smoked THC (Abrams 2007) 13 of 25 against 6 of 25, OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48); the 7 nabiximols trials together 241 of 660 against 209 of 660, OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86), I2 44.5%. Five of the 8 trials favour cannabinoids (3 significantly: Abrams 2007, Johnson 2010, Serpell 2014) and 3 favour placebo, none significantly (GW Pharmaceuticals 2005, Portenoy 2012, Selvarajah 2010). The heterogeneity P values are printed malformed, as .0.64 and .0.94; recomputed from the I2 values and the number of trials they are about .064 and .094 (editors' calculation), probably the intended values. The Discussion places the moderate-quality evidence in chronic neuropathic or cancer pain (smoked THC and nabiximols).
